title: What the Refill-Station Data Can Show
text:
Aster Manufacturing installed filtered-water refill stations in two of its six buildings as a three-month pilot. Operations manager Kenji Wu wants to expand the stations company-wide, arguing that they can reduce purchases of single-use bottled water. Before the pilot, the two test buildings ordered an average of 4,800 disposable water bottles per month. During the final month of the pilot, orders fell to 2,900 bottles.

Wu also points to the refill counters built into the stations. Together they recorded about 18,000 fills during the three months. However, the counters cannot show whether each fill replaced a disposable bottle; some employees previously used reusable bottles filled at sinks or fountains. The purchasing records are therefore more directly connected to the claim about single-use bottles than the refill count is.

The pilot also had a change that complicates the comparison. One week before the stations opened, the company stopped automatically stocking bottled water in conference rooms. Meeting organizers could still request bottles, but most began using pitchers instead. Purchasing staff estimate that conference-room orders had previously accounted for about 700 bottles per month across the two buildings.

Wu says the decline in orders is still encouraging, but he does not claim the stations caused the entire reduction. He proposes expanding to two more buildings while separately recording conference-room orders, total bottled-water purchases, maintenance costs, and station use. Finance director Alina Shah agrees the pilot is promising but says the company should not claim savings until it also compares installation and filter-replacement costs with the reduction in bottle purchases.
